scenes.heading: Number sequences
scenes.sub: Every list has a hidden rule
scenes.say: Three, four, seven, twelve, nineteen. What comes next? Sequence questions are the most common type in quantitative reasoning. Let us learn a checklist that cracks almost all of them.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Climbing stairs: look at the size of each step, not just where you are
scenes.science: In a sequence, write the gap between terms underneath
scenes.breaks: stairs always go up by the same amount. In sequences the gaps can change, double or zig-zag.
scenes.say: Think of a staircase. To know where the next step lands, look at the size of each step, not just where you stand. In a sequence, those steps are the differences. Unlike real stairs, the steps can grow, double or zig-zag.

scenes.heading: The sequence checklist
scenes.say: Work down this checklist. Differences first. If they change, find the gaps between the gaps. If numbers grow fast, try multiplying. If they zig-zag, split odd and even positions. Last, look for squares, cubes, triangular numbers, or adding the two before.

scenes.heading: Gaps that grow
scenes.question: What comes next? 3, 4, 7, 12, 19, ?
scenes.say: Three, four, seven, twelve, nineteen. The gaps are one, three, five, seven. They grow by two, so the next gap is nine. Nineteen plus nine is twenty-eight. Watch out: twenty-six repeats the old gap.
scenes.caption: Gaps 1, 3, 5, 7 grow by 2, so the next gap is 9: 19 + 9 = 28 (not 26).

scenes.heading: Two sequences woven together
scenes.question: What comes next? 1, 20, 3, 17, 9, 14, 27, ?
scenes.say: This one zig-zags. Split it. The odd places go one, three, nine, twenty-seven: times three. The even places go twenty, seventeen, fourteen: minus three. The question mark is the eighth term, an even place, so fourteen minus three is eleven.
scenes.caption: Odd places 1, 3, 9, 27 (× 3). Even places 20, 17, 14 (− 3). The 8th term is even: 14 − 3 = 11.

scenes.heading: Know your special numbers
scenes.say: Learn the special numbers so you spot them instantly: squares, cubes and triangular numbers. And remember Fibonacci-style sequences, where each term is the two before added together.

scenes.heading: Common traps

right.title: Fix
points: Test the rule on every term
Test both steps on two pairs

scenes.say: Watch for three traps. Testing only the first pair, so test every term. Repeating the last gap when the gaps are changing. And forgetting the second step of a two-step rule, like double then add one.

Quick recap. Write the gaps underneath. If they change, find the gaps of the gaps. Fast growth means multiply. Zig-zags are two sequences. And always test your rule on every term. Now try the practice questions!
